lesson.title: Why is SHA-256 irreversible?
lesson.subtitle: SHA-256 is the backbone of Bitcoin's security. Understanding why it's a one-way function — not just hard, but mathematically impossible to reverse — is fundamental to understanding how Bitcoin works.
lesson.hookLabel: The sentence "Hello, Bitcoin." — encoded as SHA-256
lesson.hookBody: That 64-character string encodes the phrase above. You cannot get the original sentence back from it — not in a trillion years. Here's the mathematical reason why.
lesson.s1p1: A hash function takes any input — a single character, a novel, an entire Bitcoin block — and produces a fixed-length fingerprint called a digest. SHA-256 always outputs exactly 256 bits, written as 64 hexadecimal characters.
lesson.s1prop1Body: "hello" always hashes to the same 64 characters. Always.
lesson.s1prop2Body: One byte or one gigabyte — the output is always 64 hex characters.
lesson.s1prop3Body: Computing a SHA-256 hash is cheap. Reversing one is not possible.
lesson.s1tryIt: Try it yourself below. Notice that any input — even nothing — always produces exactly 64 characters.
lesson.s2intro: "Irreversible" is not a practical limitation waiting for faster computers. It's baked into the mathematical structure. Three separate arguments explain why.
lesson.step1p1: SHA-256 maps an infinite set of possible inputs onto a finite set of 2²⁵⁶ outputs. By the pigeonhole principle, infinitely many inputs share every possible output hash.
lesson.step1p2: When you see a hash, you can't know which input produced it. You might find a preimage by brute force — but never the original. That information is gone.
lesson.step1callout: 2²⁵⁶ ≈ 10⁷⁷ — larger than the estimated number of atoms in the observable universe. Even checking one hash per atom per second, exhaustive search is physically impossible.
lesson.step2Title: The avalanche effect (no gradient to follow)
lesson.step2p1: Change a single character — flip one bit — and roughly half of all output bits change, apparently at random.
lesson.step2p2: There's no "getting closer." Every wrong guess looks equally wrong. Unlike a numeric equation you can solve iteratively, you have zero signal to guide a search.
lesson.step3p1: SHA-256 uses bitwise <c>XOR</c>, <c>AND</c>, <c>OR</c>, <c>bit rotation</c>, and <c>modular addition</c> — run through 64 rounds, each feeding into the next. Unlike RSA (which has a mathematical inverse) or a Caesar cipher (just reverse the shift), there is no inverse operation for SHA-256.
lesson.step3p2: Each <c>modular addition</c> discards carry information. Each <c>XOR</c> can be satisfied by two different input pairs. After 64 rounds, reconstructing the input is equivalent to solving a massively underdetermined system of equations.
lesson.s3body: Try a long paragraph, a single space, your name. No matter the size, the output is always exactly 64 hex characters — and nothing about it tells you how to find the input.
lesson.s4Body: Below is the SHA-256 hash of a short phrase. Figure out what the input was. No tricks — the only method that works is guessing.
lesson.s4callout: Even matching 63 out of 64 characters is a complete miss. That's what "preimage resistance" means — hash functions are all-or-nothing.
lesson.s5intro: SHA-256's irreversibility is not a footnote — it's the foundation Bitcoin is built on.
lesson.s5miningBody: Miners must find a block header whose hash starts with a certain number of zeros. Because hashing is irreversible, there's no shortcut — they try billions of variations per second. That brute-force effort is the "work" in Proof of Work.
lesson.s5addressBody: Your private key is hashed to produce your public address. Even though your address is visible on the blockchain, the hash ensures no one can work backwards to your private key — and your funds.
lesson.s5callout: Every Bitcoin block contains the SHA-256 hash of the previous block. This chain of hashes makes rewriting history computationally impossible — you'd have to redo the proof-of-work for every block that follows.
lesson.relatedKeys: How do public & private keys work?

howSha256.title: How does SHA-256 work?
howSha256.subtitle: SHA-256 turns any input into a 256-bit fingerprint using three deterministic phases. Tracing those steps reveals exactly why the output looks random — and why that's by design.
howSha256.hookBody: Three characters. Three phases. The 64 hex characters above are the inevitable result of running "abc" through a specific sequence of bit operations. Here's every step.
howSha256.s1intro: Every SHA-256 computation follows the same recipe. The input can be one byte or one gigabyte — the same three phases always run in the same order.
howSha256.s1phase1Body: Extend the message to an exact multiple of 512 bits using a structured pattern.
howSha256.s1phase2Body: Expand the padded block from 16 words into a 64-word schedule of mixed values.
howSha256.s1phase3Body: Run 8 working variables through 64 rounds of bit operations, then output the final 256-bit hash.
howSha256.s1tryIt: Try typing anything below. The same three phases run every time — instantly, deterministically.
howSha256.s2intro: SHA-256 processes data in 512-bit (64-byte) blocks. Before hashing begins, the message is extended to fit this block structure using a precise three-part scheme.
howSha256.step1p1: The message is encoded as bytes. ASCII text is straightforward: each character is one byte. "abc" becomes three bytes — 0x61, 0x62, 0x63.
howSha256.step1p2: The byte values are fixed by the UTF-8 standard. This step is just representation — the actual padding starts next.
howSha256.step2p1: Immediately after the last message byte, append the byte 0x80 (binary: 10000000). This marks exactly where the message ends.
howSha256.step2p2: Then append zero bytes until only 8 bytes remain in the final block. The separator guarantees that "abc" and "abc\x00" pad differently — they can't produce the same block.
howSha256.step3p1: The final 8 bytes store the original message length in bits as a 64-bit big-endian integer. "abc" is 3 bytes = 24 bits, so those last 8 bytes encode 0x0000000000000018.
howSha256.step3callout: If the message is too long to fit in one 512-bit block with the padding appended, SHA-256 uses multiple blocks — each compressed in sequence.
howSha256.step3bTitle: What happens when a message spans multiple blocks?
howSha256.step3bp1: A 512-bit block holds 64 bytes. The padding scheme needs 9 bytes of overhead (1 byte for 0x80 + 8 bytes for the length). So any message longer than 55 bytes overflows into a second block.
howSha256.step3bp2: SHA-256 handles this by chaining: after processing block 1, its output — a 256-bit internal state — becomes the starting point for block 2. Block 2 goes through the same compression step, but uses the previous block's output state instead of the fixed starting values. The final hash is the output of the last block, so every byte of every block shapes the result.
howSha256.step3bExample: Try it: type any message longer than 55 characters in the demo above — you'll see a second block appear.
howSha256.step3bChainLabel: Chaining: output of each block feeds the next
howSha256.s3intro: SHA-256 needs one input value per compression round, and there are 64 rounds. But a 512-bit padded block only gives you 16 words (16 × 32 bits = 512 bits). So SHA-256 generates 48 more by mixing the original 16 together — this is called the message schedule.
howSha256.step4p1: Read the 512-bit padded block as sixteen 32-bit chunks, labeled W[0] through W[15]. For "abc" padded, the first four bytes (0x61, 0x62, 0x63, 0x80) pack into W[0] = 0x61626380. The twelve middle words are all zeros. W[15] = 0x00000018 encodes the original message length: 24 bits.
howSha256.step5p1: For positions 16 through 63, each new word is computed from four earlier words. Two mixing functions — σ0 and σ1 — scramble inputs before adding them. Both work the same way: take a 32-bit word, rotate its bits by two different amounts, shift it once more, then XOR all three results together. The rotations ensure every output bit depends on bits from across the entire input — a single-bit change spreads to all 32 bits of the result.
howSha256.step5callout: By W[63], every word has been mixed with every other word. A single-bit change in the original message cascades through the entire 64-word schedule.
howSha256.s4intro: The compression function uses 8 working variables — a through h — and runs 64 rounds, consuming one schedule word and one round constant per round.
howSha256.step6p1: The 8 variables are set to the first 32 bits of the fractional parts of the square roots of the first 8 primes. These "nothing-up-my-sleeve" numbers prove no backdoor was inserted — anyone can verify them.
howSha256.step7p1: Each round uses one message schedule word W[i] and one of 64 round constants K[i] (derived from the cube roots of primes). Six operations mix the 8 variables each round — the same operations from the irreversibility lesson.
howSha256.step8p1: After all 64 rounds, add each working variable back to its initial H value (mod 2³²). The 8 resulting 32-bit words concatenated form the 256-bit hash.
howSha256.step8callout: Processing multiple 512-bit blocks? The output hash from one block replaces H[0]–H[7] as the initial state for the next. Every block influences the final output.
howSha256.s5intro: Bitcoin uses SHA-256 in nearly every component — typically applied twice in sequence (called SHA256d or double-SHA-256).
howSha256.s5miningBody: Miners search for a block header whose SHA256d hash starts with enough zero bits. There's no shortcut — the only method is changing the nonce and rehashing billions of times per second.
howSha256.s5txBody: Every transaction is identified by the SHA256d of its raw bytes. This TxID is what wallets and block explorers show when referencing specific transactions.
howSha256.s5merkleBody: All transactions in a block are hashed in pairs repeatedly until one root hash remains. This Merkle root lets anyone prove a transaction is in a block without downloading the whole block.
howSha256.s5addressBody: Your private key is hashed with SHA-256 (then RIPEMD-160) to produce your Bitcoin address. The hash is irreversible — your address reveals nothing about your private key.
howSha256.s5callout: SHA-256 was designed by the NSA and standardized by NIST in 2001. Its security relies entirely on the mathematical properties you just traced — not on keeping the algorithm secret.
howSha256.relatedKeys: How do public & private keys work?
howSha256.visualizerCtaBody: See every padding byte, all 64 schedule words, and each compression round — with actual values for your input.

operations.title: Operations Explorer
operations.subtitle: 8-bit demo · SHA-256 uses 32-bit
operations.rotrDesc: SHA-256 computes S0 = rotr(a,2) ^ rotr(a,13) ^ rotr(a,22). This 8-bit demo uses rotations of 1, 3, and 5 to keep it visual. Click bits to flip them.
operations.rotrWhy: A single rotation is reversible — just rotate back. But SHA-256 XORs three different rotations together. Once merged with XOR, you can't tell which bits came from which rotation. Recovering a from S0 requires solving three entangled equations simultaneously — there is no algebraic shortcut.
operations.chDesc: For each bit position: if e = 1, copy the bit from f. If e = 0, copy from g. The small label under each output bit shows which source was used.
operations.chWhy: The selector e is not present in the Ch output. Given the result and knowing f and g, you cannot recover e — you need e to know which source each bit came from, but e is exactly what you're trying to find. Swapping e and exchanging f/g produces the same Ch output from entirely different inputs.
operations.addDesc: SHA-256 uses 32-bit arithmetic (mod 2³²). This demo uses 8-bit (mod 256) so you can see the carry bit disappear. Drag the sliders until the sum overflows.
operations.addOverflow: That's ≥ 256, so the carry bit (left of divider) is discarded and the result wraps to {result}.
operations.addWhy: When the sum overflows, the carry bit is permanently gone. Given only the result {result}, you cannot reconstruct a or b — ({result}, 0) and (0, {result}) both hash to the same value, and so do every overflow pair like ({a}, {b}). SHA-256 chains 5 modular additions per round across 64 rounds, making the information loss total.
operations.majDesc: Each output bit is 1 when at least 2 of the 3 inputs are 1 — a majority vote. The small number under each result bit shows how many inputs voted 1. Click bits to experiment.
operations.majWhy: Like Ch, if you know the result is 1, you can't be sure if the inputs were (1,1,0), (1,0,1), (0,1,1), or (1,1,1). Information is lost in the 'voting' process.
operations.andExplain: AND (&): 1 only if both bits are 1.
operations.xorExplain: XOR (^): 1 if the bits are different.

roundSteps.title: Inside one SHA-256 Round
roundSteps.step1Desc: Rotate <c>e</c> by 6, 11, and 25 bits, then <c>XOR</c> them. This ensures every bit affects many others.
roundSteps.step2Desc: Use bits of <c>e</c> to choose between bits of <c>f</c> and <c>g</c>.
roundSteps.step3Desc: Sum <c>h</c>, <c>S1</c>, <c>Ch</c>, and the round's specific <c>word</c> and <c>constant</c>.
roundSteps.step4Desc: Rotate <c>a</c> by 2, 13, and 22 bits, then <c>XOR</c> them.
roundSteps.step5Desc: For each bit position, take the value that appears most often in <c>a</c>, <c>b</c>, and <c>c</c>.
roundSteps.step6Desc: Shift all values and compute new <c>a</c> and <c>e</c> for the next round.

sha256Visualizer.title: SHA-256 Visualizer
sha256Visualizer.subtitle: Type any message and trace it through every step — padding, schedule expansion, and all 64 compression rounds.
sha256Visualizer.inputNote: Supports any length — longer messages are split into multiple 512-bit blocks.
sha256Visualizer.paddingDesc: The message is padded to exactly 64 bytes (512 bits) so SHA-256 can process it as one block.
sha256Visualizer.scheduleDesc: The 64-byte padded block is split into 16 words (W[0]–W[15]). SHA-256 then generates 48 more words (W[16]–W[63]) by mixing earlier words together — one per compression round.
sha256Visualizer.sigmaExplainerDesc: Each mixes a 32-bit word using three bit operations XOR'd together — the same idea as the ROTR demo in the Operations Explorer. Three different rotations (or shifts) ensure every output bit depends on bits spread across the entire input, so a single-bit change cascades everywhere.
sha256Visualizer.scheduleClickHint: · click any word to see its formula
sha256Visualizer.workingVarsLabel: Working variables at start of round
sha256Visualizer.newStateLabel: New a and e at end of round
sha256Visualizer.compressionOverviewDesc: SHA-256 runs 64 rounds of mixing on 8 working variables (a–h). Each round pulls in two inputs: W[i], a word derived from your message (produced by the Schedule tab), and K[i], one of 64 fixed constants. The key operations are:
sha256Visualizer.compressionOverviewS1: scrambles variable e via three rotate-right XORs
sha256Visualizer.compressionOverviewCh: uses e as a bit-selector to mix f and g
sha256Visualizer.compressionOverviewT1: adds S1, Ch, h, W[i], K[i] together (mod 2³²)
sha256Visualizer.compressionOverviewS0: scrambles variable a via three rotate-right XORs
sha256Visualizer.compressionOverviewMaj: majority vote across bits of a, b, c
sha256Visualizer.compressionOverviewEnd: At the end of the round: a = T1 + T2, e = d + T1, and all other variables shift down by one slot (b←a, c←b, …).
sha256Visualizer.compExplainerSubtitle: 8-bit interactive demos that show the same ideas as the 32-bit SHA-256 operations.
sha256Visualizer.compExplainerVarsLower: (lowercase) are the eight working variables — 32-bit words that are recomputed every round.
sha256Visualizer.compExplainerVarsUpper: (uppercase) are the initial hash values (H[0]…H[7]) that are loaded into the working variables before round 0 of each block.
sha256Visualizer.compExplainerVarsAfter: After all 64 rounds, each H[i] is incremented by the final working variable: H[0] += a, H[1] += b, …, H[7] += h.
sha256Visualizer.compExplainerS1Note: Applied to working variable e. Also written Σ1 (upper-case sigma).
sha256Visualizer.compExplainerS0Note: Applied to working variable a. Also written Σ0 (upper-case sigma).
sha256Visualizer.compExplainerRotrDesc: Three right-rotations of different amounts are XOR'd together. This spreads bit influence across the whole word.
sha256Visualizer.compExplainerS1Note2: S1 (Σ1) is used in compression; the lower-case σ1 in the message schedule uses the same idea with different rotation amounts.
sha256Visualizer.compExplainerS0Note2: S0 (Σ0) is used in compression alongside S1; the lower-case σ0 in the schedule uses the same idea with different rotation amounts.
sha256Visualizer.stateFlowIVOrigin: Where do these values come from? They are the first 32 bits of the fractional part of the square root of the first 8 prime numbers. For example: √2 = 1.41421356… — take the fractional part 0.41421356… and multiply by 2³² to get 0x6a09e667. These are called "nothing-up-my-sleeve" numbers: they prove the designers did not secretly choose weak starting values.
sha256Visualizer.stateFlowMatchNote: At round 0, working vars are copied from initial H — they match exactly.
sha256Visualizer.stateFlowAddBackLabel: After 64 rounds — add back to get new H[0..7]
sha256Visualizer.stateFlowAddBackNote: New H[i] = initial H[i] + final working var (mod 2³²). This is why the hash changes completely with any input change.
sha256Visualizer.roundWNote: W[{round}] is word {round} from the Schedule tab — expanded directly from your padded message.
sha256Visualizer.roundKNote: K[{round}] is derived from the {ordinal} prime number ({prime}). The cube root <c>∛{prime} ≈ {fullValue}</c>. We take the fractional part (<c>0.{fractional}</c>), multiply it by 2³², and keep the integer portion: <c>{base10}</c> (which is <c>{hex}</c> in hex). Like the initial H values, these are "nothing-up-my-sleeve" numbers.
sha256Visualizer.hashDesc: After all 64 rounds, each working variable is added back to the initial H value. The 8 resulting 32-bit words concatenated form the 256-bit (64 hex character) hash.

publicPrivateKey.title: Public & Private Keys in Bitcoin
publicPrivateKey.subtitle: Your Bitcoin wallet is a number. Your address is a point on a curve. The relationship between them is a one-way mathematical door — trivial to open, impossible to reverse.
publicPrivateKey.hookLabel: A Bitcoin private key — generated right now in your browser
publicPrivateKey.hookBody: That 64-character number is a Bitcoin private key. Whoever knows it can sign transactions and spend the associated funds. Nobody can derive it from the public key — not even with every computer on Earth running for longer than the age of the universe.
publicPrivateKey.s1p1: A private key is just a random integer between 1 and a specific 77-digit number called the secp256k1 group order (n). Nothing more. No certificate authority, no registration — whoever generates one owns it.
publicPrivateKey.s1p2: Bitcoin uses 256-bit keys, the same size as a SHA-256 hash. There are approximately 10⁷⁷ valid private keys — one for each possible random draw from that range.
publicPrivateKey.s1prop1Body: Generated by your device using OS entropy. No one else sees this step.
publicPrivateKey.s1prop2Body: Never sent over the network. Stored encrypted in your wallet. Lose it — lose your bitcoin.
publicPrivateKey.s1prop3Body: Written as 64 hex characters or encoded as WIF (Wallet Import Format) for humans.
publicPrivateKey.s1tryIt: Generate a real private key below. Each click produces a cryptographically random number your browser has never seen before — and derives the full public key and Bitcoin address from it.
publicPrivateKey.s2Title: How the public key is derived
publicPrivateKey.step1p1: Bitcoin uses the elliptic curve y² = x³ + 7 over a prime field F_p. Points on this curve have special arithmetic — you can "add" two points to get a third, and the result is always another point on the same curve.
publicPrivateKey.step1p2: The curve has a special generator point G, hardcoded in the Bitcoin protocol. Every Bitcoin wallet uses the same G.
publicPrivateKey.step1callout: The parameters weren't chosen arbitrarily. 'secp256k1' is a standard (Certicom's SEC2) where every constant is derived from a deterministic formula — no hidden backdoor is possible.
publicPrivateKey.step2p1: Given your private key k and the generator G, your public key is: publicKey = k × G. This means adding G to itself k times. With k ≈ 10⁷⁷, that's a lot of additions — but the double-and-add algorithm does it in only ~256 steps.
publicPrivateKey.step2p2: The result is a point (x, y) on the curve, encoded as 33 bytes in compressed format: a prefix byte (02 or 03 depending on whether y is even or odd) plus the 32-byte x coordinate.
publicPrivateKey.step3p1: Finding k given only k×G is called the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP). No efficient algorithm exists for secp256k1. The best known attack — Pollard's rho — needs ~2¹²⁸ operations.
publicPrivateKey.step3code:
Forward:  k × G  →  ~256 point doublings/additions  →  milliseconds
Backward: P → k  →  ~2¹²⁸ operations                  →  physically impossible
publicPrivateKey.step3callout: Quantum computers could run Shor's algorithm to break ECDLP — but a quantum computer large enough to threaten secp256k1 does not exist. Bitcoin could migrate to post-quantum signatures if needed.
publicPrivateKey.s3Title: Try to find the private key
publicPrivateKey.s3body: Below is the public key of a small curve. The math is identical to secp256k1 — just with a much smaller prime field so you can actually try every possibility.
publicPrivateKey.s3callout: You can find the key by trying k = 1, 2, 3… because this toy curve has fewer than 50 points. secp256k1 has 2²⁵⁶ possible private keys. The same exhaustive search would take 10⁵⁸ years.
publicPrivateKey.s4Title: From public key to Bitcoin address
publicPrivateKey.step4ap1: A Bitcoin address is not the public key itself — it's two hash functions applied in sequence: SHA-256, then RIPEMD-160. This produces a 20-byte (160-bit) address hash.
publicPrivateKey.step4ap2: Why hash? It shortens the address and adds a second layer of security. Even if elliptic curve cryptography were broken someday, an attacker would also need to break two hash functions simultaneously.
publicPrivateKey.step4aCode:
step 1: SHA256(publicKey)             → 32 bytes
step 2: RIPEMD160(result)              → 20 bytes  (address hash)
step 3: prepend version byte (0x00 mainnet)
step 4: checksum = SHA256(SHA256(versioned))[0:4]
step 5: Base58Check(versioned + checksum)  → human-readable address
publicPrivateKey.step4bTitle: Why addresses can receive but not prove ownership
publicPrivateKey.step4bp1: Anyone can send bitcoin to your address — they just need the 20-byte hash. But to spend it, you must prove you know the private key that produced the public key that hashes to that address. That proof is a digital signature.
publicPrivateKey.step4bcallout: Your address appears on the blockchain every time someone sends you bitcoin. But it reveals nothing about your private key — or even your full public key (until you spend from it).
publicPrivateKey.step4cp1: Every step is one-way. You can share your address and public key publicly. The private key stays private — that is the entire security model.
publicPrivateKey.s5intro: Public-key cryptography is the reason Bitcoin has no passwords, no accounts, and no bank.
publicPrivateKey.s5ownershipBody: There are no accounts in Bitcoin. Owning bitcoin means knowing a private key. No bank can freeze it, no government can seize it without that number.
publicPrivateKey.s5sigBody: When you spend bitcoin, you create an ECDSA signature using your private key. Nodes verify it against your public key — proving you authorized the transaction without revealing the key.
publicPrivateKey.s5hdBody: Modern wallets derive billions of key pairs from one master seed using BIP32. One backup phrase unlocks infinite addresses, all derived deterministically.
publicPrivateKey.s5quantumBody: ECDLP is theoretically vulnerable to Shor's algorithm on a future quantum computer. Bitcoin addresses that have never spent (public key unrevealed) have an extra hash layer of protection.
publicPrivateKey.s5callout: Every Bitcoin transaction ever made is a mathematical proof of private key ownership — verified in milliseconds by thousands of nodes worldwide, without any trusted third party.

multisig.title: How Multisig Wallets Work
multisig.subtitle: One key is one point of failure. A multisig wallet splits control across several keys and lets Bitcoin's own script language enforce how many of them must agree before a single satoshi moves.
multisig.hookLabel: A 2-of-3 vault — two signatures unlock it, the third key stays offline
multisig.hookBody: This vault holds bitcoin behind three keys but only needs two signatures to spend. Lose one key and your money is still safe. Have one key stolen and the thief still can't move anything. That rule isn't enforced by a company — it's written into the transaction itself and re-checked by every node on the network.
multisig.s1p1: A normal Bitcoin wallet is protected by one private key. That single number is the entire security model: whoever has it can spend, and whoever loses it loses the funds forever. There is no reset link and no support desk.
multisig.s1p2: A multisig (multi-signature) wallet replaces that one key with N keys plus a rule: at least M of them must sign before the coins move. Written M-of-N — 2-of-3, 3-of-5, 2-of-2. The keys can live in different places, on different devices, held by different people.
multisig.s1prop1Body: A 2-of-3 vault doesn't need all three keys — any two are enough, and it doesn't matter which two.
multisig.s1prop2Body: Each key is a completely separate private key with its own seed phrase. Compromising one reveals nothing about the others.
multisig.s1prop3Body: The rule lives in the Bitcoin script that locks the coins, and every node re-checks it. No custodian, no company policy, no trust required.
multisig.s1callout: Multisig has been part of Bitcoin since 2012 (BIP 11 and BIP 16). It isn't a wallet feature bolted on top — it's a spending condition the base protocol understands natively.
multisig.s2Title: How it works, step by step
multisig.s2intro: Three things have to happen: the rule gets baked into an address, each cosigner signs the same transaction, and the network verifies the signatures that were collected.
multisig.step1p1: A multisig address is created from a small program called a redeem script (or witness script for SegWit). It lists the public keys and the threshold, and ends with the OP_CHECKMULTISIG opcode.
multisig.step1code:
OP_2                       // threshold M = 2
  <02a1b2...c3>            // cosigner 1 public key
  <03d4e5...f6>            // cosigner 2 public key
  <02789a...bc>            // cosigner 3 public key
OP_3                       // total keys N = 3
OP_CHECKMULTISIG
multisig.step1p2: That script is then hashed — HASH160 for a P2SH address starting with 3, SHA-256 for a P2WSH address starting with bc1q — and the hash becomes the address. Anyone can send to it without knowing it's a multisig, because all they ever see is a hash.
multisig.step1callout: Because the address is a hash of the script, changing the threshold from 2-of-3 to 3-of-3 — or even reordering the public keys — produces a completely different address. The rule is locked in the moment the address is created.
multisig.step2Title: Each cosigner signs the same transaction
multisig.step2p1: To spend, someone drafts an unsigned transaction: which coins to spend, where they go, what fee to pay. Every cosigner then signs that exact transaction with their own private key using ECDSA over secp256k1 — the same signature scheme a single-key wallet uses.
multisig.step2p2: The draft travels between cosigners as a PSBT (Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction, BIP 174). Each device adds its signature and passes it along. The private keys never leave their devices and never meet.
multisig.step2code:
1. coordinator  -> creates unsigned PSBT
2. hardware key -> adds signature 1  -> PSBT (1 of 2)
3. laptop key   -> adds signature 2  -> PSBT (2 of 2)
4. anyone       -> finalizes and broadcasts
multisig.step3p1: The spending transaction reveals the redeem script alongside the collected signatures. Every node hashes the script to confirm it matches the address, then runs OP_CHECKMULTISIG: it walks the signature list against the public key list and requires M valid signatures, given in the same order the keys were listed.
multisig.step3code:
input script:  OP_0 '<sig1>' '<sig2>' '<redeemScript>'

hash(redeemScript) == address hash ?   -> yes
valid signatures found             ?   -> 2 of 3
2 >= threshold (2)                 ?   -> accepted
multisig.step3callout: That leading OP_0 is a real bug in the original implementation: OP_CHECKMULTISIG pops one item too many off the stack. It can never be fixed without a hard fork, so every multisig spend in Bitcoin's history carries that extra dummy value.
multisig.s3Title: Try it: spend from a 2-of-3 vault
multisig.s3body: Below is a working multisig vault. Three keypairs are generated in your browser, a genuine redeem script and P2SH address are derived from them, and each Sign button produces a real ECDSA signature over the transaction. Collect enough valid signatures and the spend goes through — then tamper with the amount and watch what happens.
multisig.s3callout: A signature commits to the exact transaction: amount, destination, fee. Change one character and every signature collected so far becomes invalid. That's why a compromised coordinator can't redirect your money — it can rewrite the draft, but the cosigners' signatures won't survive the edit.
multisig.s4body: The threshold is a dial between two failure modes. A high M makes theft harder; a low M makes loss survivable. Move the sliders to see the trade-off run in both directions.
multisig.s4callout: Backing up the seed phrases is not enough. To rebuild a multisig wallet you also need the wallet descriptor (or the full redeem script) — the threshold and every public key in the right order. Without it the funds are unspendable even if you hold every private key.
multisig.s5intro: Multisig turns “don't lose your key” from a single catastrophic risk into an engineering problem you can design around.
multisig.s5custodyTitle: Self-custody without a single point of failure
multisig.s5custodyBody: A 2-of-3 split across a home safe, a hardware wallet, and a distant backup survives a house fire, a stolen device, or a burglary — any one of them — without losing the coins.
multisig.s5treasuryBody: A 3-of-5 across executives means no single employee can move company funds, and no single departure or compromise locks the treasury.
multisig.s5inheritanceBody: Give one key to a family member or a recovery service. They can't spend alone, but combined with your backup they can recover the funds if you're gone.
multisig.s5taprootBody: Since Taproot (2021), cosigners can combine their keys into one aggregated signature. On-chain it looks like an ordinary single-key spend — cheaper in fees, and private about the policy behind it.
multisig.s5callout: Multisig is the clearest example of what Bitcoin's script layer buys you: a spending policy no institution has to be trusted to honour, because thousands of independent nodes re-verify it on every single transaction.

multisigConfig.label: {m}-of-{n}
multisigConfig.diagramCaption: Highlighted keys are the minimum needed to spend
multisigConfig.attackerBody: An attacker needs {m} of your {n} keys. Anything less and the funds stay locked.
multisigConfig.lossBody: You can lose {canLose} of {n} keys and still recover everything.
multisigConfig.lossBodyNone: Every key is required. Lose one and the funds are gone forever.
multisigConfig.noRedundancy: M equals N, so there is no recovery margin at all. This suits escrow between parties who both must agree, not personal savings.
multisigConfig.noSecurity: A threshold of 1 lets any single key spend on its own. Convenient for shared spending, but against theft it's no better than a single-key wallet.
